Photograph: Marek Ladzinski/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov speaks to reporters after his address at the UN general assembly in New York. Photograph: Marek Ladzinski/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: German foreign minister urges Russia to abandon dangerous escalation in rare meeting The two foreign ministers met on the sidelines of the UN general assembly in New York even though relations have been frozen since the invasion. What we know on day 1,677 Guardian staff and agencies Sat 26 Sep 2026 22.30 EDT Last modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 22.32 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The foreign ministers of Russia and Germany met in New York on the sidelines of the ⁠UN general assembly , ⁠in the first such ​talks since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine . But Russia’s top diplomat dismissed Germany’s calls to ease off its “dangerous path of escalation” toward Europe, instead accusing Germany of being Ukraine’s main sponsor and seeking to be a leading military power in Europe. “Does Berlin understand what this could lead to?” the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, asked in his speech at the gathering of world leaders on Saturday. “Didn’t they learn the lessons of world war two?” German foreign minister, Johann ‌Wadephul, used the talks to call on Russia “to abandon the dangerous path of escalation vis-a-vis Germany, Europe, and Nato” , according to a delegation source. Wadephul said incidents such as the attempted drone attack in Leipzig would not shake Germany’s resolve to support Ukraine, according to sources. Relations between Moscow and Berlin have been frozen since the Russian invasion , and tensions escalated further after the drone incident at Leipzig airport. In a sign of the continued frostiness, Lavrov told a press conference on Saturday “nothing new” came from the talks with his German counterpart. “I told him that frankly … you could just have called me and said: ‘read my statement’,” Lavrov said . “He simply reiterated his official public position condemning Russia … you can judge for yourself whether that counts as dialogue or not.” Kyiv has become a frontline city - and winter is on the way Read more Still, the ​ministers discussed bilateral ties and the war in Ukraine, officials from ‌both sides said. Wadephul urged Lavrov to do “everything possible to reach an agreement on grain exports via the Black Sea”, a German ‌delegation source said. In a sign of the sensitivities around meeting the Russian foreign minister , Wadephul notified his European allies of the meeting afterwards in a message seen by Reuters. “I used this opportunity to reiterate our position on Russia’s war of aggression ⁠against Ukraine and to call for an immediate and complete ceasefire, most pressingly with a focus on grain ​exports, and the energy infrastructure,” he wrote. After the meeting Lavrov addressed world leaders at the assembly, where he defended Russia’s war in Ukraine and lobbed barbs at the west — including Germany – and criticised the militarisation of Japan. He made clear that Russia will veto any attempt by Germany and Japan for permanent seats on the UN security council. The two nations fought Russia, Britain and the US in the second world war. Writing on her personal Telegram channel, Maria Zakharova, a spokesperson for Russia’s foreign ministry, said that “tens of diplomats” had come to meet Lavrov to “shake his hand and thank Russia”. An overwhelming majority of general assembly member nations have repeatedly condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine , as Wadephul noted in his own address to the assembly Saturday. “Russia’s war targets the lives of millions of innocent people, the existence of the Ukrainian state and culture and the European peace order,” he said, urging Russia to negotiating toward ending the fighting. The talks came amid an intensifying aerial war and as Donald Trump said he hoped the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, would “settle” with Russia’s Vladimir Putin. With frontline positions largely unchanged since last year, Russia has hammered Ukraine with cruise and ballistic missiles, powerful glide bombs and jet-powered drones in recent months, while Ukraine’s long-range drones have targeted Russian oil refineries and businesses. “It is essential that our partners not forget: Russia is escalating every single day,” Zelenskyy wrote on Saturday. “If the Russians have chosen to make their strikes even more brutal, the world must choose stronger responses to keep the war from spreading further.” Ukrainian officials said Russian attacks killed four people on Saturday, as Russian authorities said a Ukrainian drone attack killed three. Residents of Kyiv are preparing for power cuts, drone attacks and a bitter cold winter by stocking up on generators, food and “dry showers”, as the Ukrainian capital becomes a frontline city . And Russia has opened a new front in its campaign against Ukraine , hitting several datacentres and internet providers in Kyiv this week in an apparent attempt to weaken the digital backbone of the economy. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: ‘In some sense, Mr Trump was too successful in the first year and didn’t sell it enough in the second year.’ Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images View image in fullscreen ‘In some sense, Mr Trump was too successful in the first year and didn’t sell it enough in the second year.’ Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images Republicans Analysis Conservative media weighs its future as cracks emerge in Trump’s movement Jeremy Barr in Washington Two weeks after Democrats flipped Congress, conservative outlets are having conversations on whether to distance themselves from Trump or double down on Maga Sun 22 Nov 2026 06.00 EST Last modified on Sun 22 Nov 2026 06.01 EST Share As a so-called “blue wave” crashed across the country on the night of 3 November, conservative hosts and commentators on Fox News displayed an almost virtuosic ability to avoid directly blaming Donald Trump for the Republican party’s defeat, instead pinning the blame on impertinent voters who didn’t grasp the strength of the economy. “In some sense, Mr Trump was too successful in the first year and didn’t sell it enough in the second year,” said Larry Kudlow, a Fox Business Network host who served as the president’s director of the National Economic Council during his first administration. But two weeks on, Trump’s electoral wipeout is facilitating difficult conversations about the future of the conservative media ecosystem – and whether outlets that target a Republican-voting audience need to create some distance from an unpopular president. Some other outlets, like the Maga-aligned Real America’s Voice News network, are planning to go the other direction and double down on Trump. View image in fullscreen FOX Business anchor Larry Kudlow at Fox Business Network studios on 16 January in New York City. Photograph: John Lamparski/Getty Images “The whole landscape can now be reordered, and I think it will be,” said Steve Bannon, a former chief strategist to Trump during his first administration who now hosts a show for Real America’s Voice. Several conservative media personalities pinned the blame on Fox News for leading the party – and Trump – astray, with former host Tucker Carlson saying that the results signaled the end of “the Fox News era”. (Carlson didn’t respond to a message seeking comment.) Bannon, who contends that Rupert Murdoch has long “hated Trump”, predicted that the network will utilize the party’s recent “rejection” at the polls to move away from Trump and embrace more traditional, George W Bush-era Republican priorities. “They’re going to try to kick Trump into the dustbin,” he said. “They clearly have moved beyond Trump and they want to move beyond Trumpism … What they’re going to do is, with a thousand cuts, convince their ageing audience that Maga and what Maga stands for is too extreme.” In contrast, Bannon said he expects Real America’s Voice and other outlets to “triple down” on the Maga movement and “populist nationalism.” Bannon is not alone in his criticism of Murdoch’s media empire. Conservative commentator Ann Coulter said that she views the channel and its sister outlet, the New York Post, as “90% responsible for the GOP wipeout in the midterm elections”, blaming voices in the Murdoch media empire for encouraging Trump to launch – and sustain – an unpopular war against Iran. View image in fullscreen Steve Bannon speaks at the Conservative Political Action Conference at the Gaylord Texan Resort and Convention Center, in Grapevine, Texas, on 27 March. Photograph: Callaghan O’Hare/Reuters Atlanta-based conservative radio host Erick Erickson said a realignment away from Trump will probably start in his medium before it carries over to conservative television – though he said it will take time, and will depend on how important access is for certain personalities. “The more often you spend time at Mar-a-Lago, the less likely you are to distance yourself from Trump, because you still want in,” said Erickson, who vocally opposed Trump in 2016 before coming around ahead of his 2020 re-election bid. Charlie Sykes, a former conservative radio host who also opposed Trump from the beginning, said the election has shown “cracks in that alternative reality silo” on Trump-aligned channels and platforms. “In general, I think the scope of the blowout was just so great that even deep in the rightwing media ecosystem, they had to feel the tremors of it,” said Sykes, a former MS Now commentator who now writes on Substack . “And so that has been kind of interesting, this sense of like, ‘OK, we need to really come to grips with this and maybe figure out a way to move on.’” Trump’s decision to attack Iran in February fomented division within the conservative media ecosystem, with many commentators viewing it as an abdication of his promise to abstain from foreign wars and focus on the US. “I think those divisions are just going to widen,” Sykes said. The Daily Caller, which was co-founded by Carlson in 2010 as something of a conservative alternative to the New York Times, made waves ahead of the midterms for calling out Trump’s war against Iran – and the high prices that have come out of it. “The Daily Caller is clearly positioning itself for a landscape not just post-midterms but post-Trump, and for a bitter and intensifying intraparty media battle,” the digital publication Semafor wrote on 1 November. View image in fullscreen Tucker Carlson speaks at his Live Tour at the Desert Diamond Arena on 31 October 2024 in Phoenix, Arizona. Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images In an interview, Daily Caller editor-in-chief Amber Duke said the publication is more focused on reflecting the mood of the American people – particularly younger people affected by a challenging economy – than boosting Trump and the Maga movement. “I think what we are doing is so unique that we are really setting ourselves apart,” she said. “We view ourselves as a principled, America-first outlet. I think there’s a difference between Maga and America-first.” Duke also acknowledged the economic opportunities that drive support for the president. “Trump is a content goldmine. He drives a lot of traffic, a lot of clicks,” she said. “That content mine is eventually going to dry up. I would definitely be concerned if I had my entire business model tied around this uniquely celebrity-oriented newsmaker. How am I going to continue to stay in business after that? For us, it’s: Let’s just tell the truth to the American people, and that truth is not going to be dependent on any one person or political party.” Some conservative outlets that are closely tied to Trump, however, don’t see any reason to do anything differently. “Nothing changes with us,” Newsmax chief executive Christopher Ruddy said. “We’re going to continue reporting on the administration and we will continue to cover the Congress. We make a very concerted effort to always get both sides on our reports and in our TV opinion segments.” View image in fullscreen Christopher Ruddy, chief executive officer of Newsmax, speaks during the Conservative Political Action Conference in National Harbor, Maryland, on 2 March 2023. Photograph: Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images Charles Herring, president of the far-right One America News Network, echoed that sentiment: “Our reporting doesn’t change based on the political pendulum or who resides in the White House. We are working hard every day to further enhance our coverage for our viewers.” Still, there are limits to how far some conservative media organizations can stray from the president, considering the economic imperative to retain a pro-Trump audience. “The thing to understand about conservative media is that it’s not necessarily always top down,” Sykes said. “It’s often: What will the audience tolerate? … Nobody wants to get too crosswise with their audience.” But the vast majority of conservative news sites have already seen declines in online traffic in recent months , according to industry tracker Howard Polskin, an early warning sign for the party’s midterm chances. “Audiences are not buying what Maga media is selling anymore,” he said. “My prediction would be that in the next two years, rightwing media will become fractured with more infighting, breaking into two camps: pro-Maga/Trump and anti-Maga/Trump,” Polskin added. “Traffic to rightwing websites will continue to nose dive, much more so than mainstream media.” Several conservative media veterans who spoke with the Guardian said the selection of a 2028 Republican presidential nominee will probably be a defining moment for the sector, and one that could split conservative media into different camps. On the notion that vice-president JD Vance will be Trump’s heir apparent, Erickson said: “I actually am kind of encouraged by the level of pushback after the election that maybe this isn’t a good idea.” Brian Kilmeade, the co-host of the influential Fox News morning show Fox & Friends, has been particularly critical of Vance for seeming to distance himself from Trump’s decision-making on Iran. On his radio show this past week , Kilmeade said that Vance “never should have been vice-president” and that he’s “amazed that President Trump puts up with it”. View image in fullscreen Brian Kilmeade is seen on Fox & Friends at Fox News Channel Studios in New York City on 21 July 2025. Photograph: Noam Galai/Getty Images Over the next two years, conservative media personalities will have to put their chips down on a candidate. The challenge, Sykes said, is “figuring out where the audience is going, and getting there first”. He also expects conservative media outlets to prioritize attacking Democrats and undermining their control of Congress. “It’s no longer about defense of Trump,” he added. “It’s like: What’s next? And everybody’s got to make that pivot.” Explore more on these topics Republicans TV news Donald Trump US politics Fox Fox News US television industry analysis Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
